title: Back to the river bank
body: Which parts of this prefix would help you choose a continuation?

title: Three heads can keep three readings separate
body: One head could favour red, another wool, another hooded. Each receives the same input rows but can return a different weighted message. The output projection combines those messages.
companion: This is a possible division of work, not three manually assigned jobs. All three heads see all seven rows, including coat. Head-specific projections can expose different matching and value features. A single head may also encode several attributes; the extra capability is independent source weighting, not a rule that each head can understand only one concept.

title: One head gives “the” one weighted message
body: One query chooses how much to read from each token. The head mixes their value vectors into one message for the final “the”.
companion: The prefix is “The fisherman sat beside the river bank and watched the ___”. The final known token, the at slot 10, is the receiver. The blank has no query yet. One head can read several words and carry several features in its message. It uses one shared set of source weights for all coordinates of that message. “Setting clues?” describes a possible role of the numerical query, not a literal question or a manually assigned task.

title: Two heads give “the” two separate messages
body: Same receiver, two queries. Each head has its own keys, values and weights. One can favour river, the other fisherman. We combine their messages afterward.
companion:
Each head learns its own W_Q, W_K and W_V, applied to the same input rows. At this receiver that produces one query per head. Both heads can read all ten known tokens and run in parallel. Training can discover useful roles, but does not assign setting and person labels or guarantee that the heads specialize this way.

Optional: why separate weights can help

In a separate two-source toy, let river have value [10, 1] and fisherman [2, 8]. A single head with weights [0.8, 0.2] returns [8.4, 2.4]. Both coordinates use that same mixture. Two heads can instead select one value coordinate each: a setting head with weights [0.8, 0.2] gives 8.4, and a person head with weights [0.2, 0.8] gives 6.6. With these fixed values, one river weight cannot be both 0.8 and 0.2. This illustrates independent source weighting, not a proof that every one-head network fails. These invented numbers are separate from the full-sentence worksheet that follows.

title: The same roles in the river example
body: Same sentence, separate readings. Each head learns its own queries, keys and values.
companion: These are possible roles, not assigned jobs or measured explanations of the trained heads. The prefix is “The fisherman sat beside the river bank and watched the ___”. Each head sees every allowed source.

title: Keep both messages, then combine them
body: Concatenation joins the coordinates. The output projection learns how both heads contribute to the update.

title: The complete multi-head model
body: Both heads read the same E. Their messages combine; the final updated row predicts the next token.
companion:
H = AV is the message matrix. This diagram keeps the two-head worksheet dimensions: 10 tokens, width 4, two heads of width 2. Next we switch to the trained TinyStories model: 64 slots, width 64, four heads of width 16.

Optional: every worked calculation and the interactive head explorer · Executable Notebook 7.

title: Now learn from TinyStories
body: Our subset has 6,000 short, synthetic stories. Split whole stories before making next-token windows.
companion: TinyStories by Ronen Eldan and Yuanzhi Li, CDLA-Sharing-1.0. This is a 6,000-document subset, not the complete dataset. The saved split audit reports zero document overlap. Read a complete source story and its provenance.

title: Use one vocabulary for all three models
body: PAD: padding · BOS: beginning of story · EOS: end of story · UNK: unknown token.
companion: The vocabulary is fitted on training stories only. The tokenizer separates punctuation too; “word” is shorthand for a vocabulary token. BOS/EOS wrap a complete story, not each sentence. Left-pad short prefixes, crop long prefixes to their last 64 tokens, and never cross a story boundary.

title: The next word is the target, not an input
body: Slide the boundary one token forward to make another example. Each example still occupies 64 slots.
companion: Lily’s sentence is an authored teaching example, not a claimed source story. The IDs here use the actual 4,000-item benchmark vocabulary. PAD is ID 0. These two rows illustrate batching; the saved training runs use batches of 512. Position IDs are 0–63 within each padded/cropped window.

title: 1 · Look up rows, add positions, make Q/K/V
body: Now use 64 slots, width 64 and four heads of width 16. B counts examples: two above, 512 per training batch.
code:
E = token_embedding(X) + position_embedding(positions)
Q, K, V = (split_heads(layer(E)) for layer in (W_Q, W_K, W_V))

title: 2 · Match, mask, then normalize
body: The four heads form four different attention patterns. Targets never enter this calculation.
companion: This is the full causal teaching view for real receiver rows. The implementation keeps PAD-only receiver rows numerically defined; they do not feed the loss. The saved training and browser forward path computes only the final receiver’s query, since this task predicts one next token per window. It produces the same final logits with smaller [B,4,1,64] weight tensors.

title: 3 · Mix values, join heads, add the update
body: Each head sends its own message. Joining four 16-coordinate messages restores width 64.
code:
messages = A @ V
joined = messages.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, 64, 64)
updated = E + W_O(joined)

title: 4 · Predict the target from the final row
body: “BOS lily found” → target a. “BOS lily found a” → target red. The model supplies scores; the story supplies the answers.
code:
logits = vocab_head(relu(hidden_layer(updated[:, -1])))
loss = cross_entropy(logits, y)  # raw logits, observed next-token IDs

title: 5 · One loss trains the whole model
body: Token rows, position rows, all heads, the output projection and the prediction MLP learn together.
companion: We do not assign head-specific targets such as “setting” or “person”. All heads learn through the same next-token task. These are one-block teaching models, not a full stack of normalized Transformer blocks.

title: 6 · Generate with fixed parameters
body: Training changes the weights. Generation keeps the weights fixed and grows the prefix.
companion: The app excludes PAD, BOS and UNK as generated outputs; EOS may end the story. The same tokenizer and vocabulary are used for training and generation. Attention softmax chooses source positions; vocabulary softmax supplies next-token probabilities.

title: Change the model, keep the task fixed
body: Same 6,000 stories, vocabulary, context and 6,000-update budget. Three seeds: 11, 29, 47. Select by validation loss; evaluate on test stories.
companion: Both attention models add learned position rows, use the same total width and prediction MLP, and have equal parameter counts. The MLP has no separate position table: concatenation encodes slot order. Four heads reuse the single-head optimizer settings. This is not a position-encoding ablation or a parameter-matched MLP comparison.

title: Watch validation loss fall
body: Saved measurements from seed 11. Choose the best validation checkpoint—not simply the last update.
companion: These are fixed selection-slice validation measurements, not test losses. The table on the next slide aggregates separately selected test checkpoints across three seeds. All traces, checkpoint choices and protocol.

title: Four heads win this held-out comparison
body: Mean ± sample SD across three seeds. Four heads reduce mean perplexity by 8.2% versus one head in this experiment.
companion: Loss is next-token cross-entropy in nats; each run’s perplexity is exp(loss), then the table averages the run perplexities. Lower means more probability assigned to observed tokens. It is not an accuracy percentage or a guarantee for every prompt.

title: Better prediction has a cost
body: Mean training time, including validation, on Apple M2 Max/MPS. The attention models have equal parameter counts; four heads train slightly slower.
companion: Mean wall-clock training time, including validation, on Apple M2 Max / MPS. Times are device-specific. For full-sequence attention at fixed width D, matching and mixing cost O(T²D) for either head count; storing all weights costs O(hT²). The optimized next-token path used here computes only the final query. Open measured size, loss and timing results · Optional complexity derivation.

title: The same prompt, three actual continuations
body: Saved seed-11 checkpoints · greedy decoding · 24-token limit. Four heads keep “owl” in view here, but all three outputs still have flaws.
companion: Unedited saved outputs for the app’s held-out preset. It was chosen as the shortest test document, not selected for an attractive output. Aggregate loss is stronger evidence than one sample. The app lets students inspect more prompts and generate fresh continuations.
